food.text: Under the Ajuran Sultanate, farms in the Jubba and Shabelle valleys grew more productive with centralized supervision. Irrigation ditches called Kelliyo carried water from the Shebelle and Jubba rivers into plantations growing sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton.

In the 16th century, Duarte Barbosa noted that ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya sailed to Mogadishu with cloths and spices, and received gold, wax and ivory in return. He also highlighted the abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses and fruit on the coastal markets, which generated enormous wealth for the merchants.

The coffee plant originates in the Ethiopian region of Kaffa. According to legend, the 9th-century goat herder Kaldi discovered it after noticing the energizing effect it had on his flock, but this story did not appear in writing until 1671.

Farming communities of the hinterland brought their products to the coastal cities of Merca, Mogadishu and Barawa, where they were sold to local merchants. These merchants kept up foreign commerce with ships sailing to and from Arabia, India, Venice, Persia, Egypt, Portugal, and as far as China.

The Ajuran irrigation system was supported by numerous dikes and dams. The Ajuran Sultanate was described as Africa's only 'hydraulic empire', a reputation built on controlling water for its farms along the Shebelle and Jubba rivers.

Ethiopian Christians refrained from drinking coffee until the 19th century because of its perceived association with Muslims. This was despite coffee having originated in Ethiopia, in the region of Kaffa.

Ajuran crops were grown during the gu (Spring) and xagaa (Summer) seasons of the Somali calendar. To determine the average size of a farm, a land measurement system was invented, with moos, taraab and guldeed as its terms.

art.text: In 1636, Emperor Fasilides founded Gondar as a permanent capital. The period saw profound achievements in Ethiopian art and architecture, including the royal complex Fasil Ghebbi and 44 churches established around Lake Tana.

Gondarine artists created diptychs, triptychs, murals and illuminated manuscripts, mostly with religious motifs. The Ethiopian Empire's Early Modern period has been described as one of intense cultural and artistic creation.

Ethiopian music is divided between secular zafan and sacred zema. Tradition credits Yared with the hymns and the notation system called meleket, but a 16th-century royal chronicle credits two clerics with the system instead.

Portuguese Jesuit missionaries arrived in the 16th and 17th centuries, bringing Baroque, Arab, Turkish and Gujarati Indian influences into Ethiopian architecture. Portuguese soldiers had first come in the mid-16th century as allies against Adal.

In the 18th century, the Swahili town of Pate enjoyed a "Golden Age" in the fine arts. Builders made some of the finest houses on the coast with elaborate plasterwork, goldsmiths made intricate jewellery, weavers made fine cloths including silks, and carpenters made fine wooden furniture.

When the Yemeni ambassador Hassan ibn Ahmad al-Haymi visited Emperor Fasilides' new stone palace at Gondar in 1648, he called it one of the marvellous buildings and the most beautiful of outstanding wonders. The palace had been designed by an Indian architect named Abdal Kerim.

Emperor Iyasu I's palace at Gondar, nicknamed the Saddle on Horseback for its shape, celebrated his skill as a horseman. He decorated it with ivory, mirrors, cedar wood, and a ceiling covered in gold leaf and precious stones.

The church of Mekane Selassie in the Amhara region, begun by Emperor Naod and finished by his son Lebna Dengel, measured some 150 feet by 150 feet. Francisco Alvarez, who had visited it earlier, confirmed that it was wholly covered in gold leaf and inlaid with gems, pearls and corals. In 1531 the church, along with a large number of monasteries in the region, was sacked and burned down by the invasion led by Ahmad bin Ibrahim.

Castle building in Ethiopia began especially under Sarsa Dengel around the Lake Tana region. Later emperors kept the tradition, which eventually produced the Fasil Ghebbi, the royal enclosure of castles, in the new capital Gondar in 1636.
Emperor Susenyos converted to Catholicism in 1622 and declared it the state religion from 1624. He employed Arab, Gujarati and Jesuit masons alongside local masons, some of whom were Beta Israel.

In the Gondarine period, artists created diptychs and triptychs, murals and illuminated manuscripts, mostly with religious motifs. The Early Modern period is described as one of intense cultural and artistic creation in Ethiopia.

Emperor Iyasu I's palace at Gondar was nicknamed the "Saddle on Horseback" because it resembles a saddle, highlighting the emperor's horsemanship. Iyasu decorated it with ivory, mirrors, cedar, and a ceiling covered in gold leaf and precious stones.

The Indian architect Abdal Kerim designed Emperor Fasilides' stone palace at Gondar, but he had already built a palace for Emperor Susenyos I at Danqaz before that. This detail comes from the Yemeni ambassador Hassan ibn Ahmad al-Haymi, who visited Gondar in 1648.

Emperor Yohannes I died in July 1682, after living for only ten days in a great new building at Gondar that had been constructed that very year. According to the chronicles, the building was ornamented in ivory and built by an Ethiopian architect named Walda Giyorgis, described as "able, intelligent, and of good renown."

Pedro Páez also worked as a builder. At Gorgora on Lake Tana he built a stone church, dedicated on 16 January 1621, and some Catholic churches he designed still stand around Bahir Dar and Gondar. They influenced Ethiopian architecture for the rest of the 17th century.

A Yemeni ambassador, Hassan ibn Ahmad al-Haymi, visited the palace of Fasilides in 1648, when it was only a few years old. He called it a great house of stone and lime and said the architect was an Indian named Abdal Kerim, who had earlier worked on Emperor Susenyos I's palace at Danqaz.

Under Fasilides most foreign builders were expelled, yet some of their architectural styles were absorbed into the prevailing Ethiopian style. This Gondarine style persisted throughout the 17th and 18th centuries.

Gondarine architecture was limited to royalty. In 1684 the Yemeni ambassador Hassan ibn Ahmed Al Haymi noted that apart from the Fasil Ghebbi, the rest of Gondar was made of tukuls, which he called "nets of grass".
The Friday mosque of Merca, built in 1609, was for centuries one of only three mosques in East Africa with minarets. The others were Arba'a Rukun and Fakr ad-Din, both dated to 1269.
The use and production of the siwa, a musical instrument, were among the most famous things about Pate in its Golden Age. Two examples of siwas are held in the museum in Lamu.

The stonework of Fasilides' palace at Gondar was built mainly by local Ethiopian Jews known as the Beta Israel, especially the Kayla clan, who traditionally worked as masons, metalsmiths and carpenters. These skilled trades were nevertheless looked down upon by the wider Ethiopian population at the time.
The royal chronicles say the buildings of Yohannes I and Iyasu I at Gondar were built by an Ethiopian architect named Walda Giyorgis, described as "able, intelligent, and of good renown."

In 1709, Wallo Oromo raiders invaded the Amba of Atronsa Maryam in Saynt, a prominent royal monastery. They scattered its historic relics, killed its clergy and carried away women and children as prisoners. They also tossed the disputed picture of the Virgin and Child over the steep cliff, along with the bones of the fifteenth-century Emperor Ba'eda Maryam, who was buried there.

war.text: The Ethiopian–Adal War pitted the Christian Ethiopian Empire against the Muslim Adal Sultanate from 1529 to 1543. Adal's forces included Harla/Harari, Somali, Afar, Arab and Turkish gunmen. Under Imam Ahmad, they came close to extinguishing the ancient Ethiopian kingdom, slaughtering any Ethiopian who refused to convert to Islam and wreaking havoc on the Christian nation. By the war's close, the Christian side was supported by the Portuguese Empire with no less than 400 musketeers.

Ethiopian infantry and cavalry universally carried the sword and spear, and cavalry were often equipped with chain mail and helmets. The bow and arrow were widespread, and arrow poison was occasionally used. Ethiopia's first experience with firearms was the Ethiopian–Adal War, which saw guns used on both sides.

On 21 February 1543, east of Lake Tana, a combined Ethiopian and Portuguese army led by Emperor Galawdewos defeated the Adal-Ottoman army of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi. Imam Ahmad was hit by a bullet to the chest that threw him from his horse and was killed, though the sources differ on how he died. His routed followers were cut down by the Ethiopians and Portuguese as they ran back to their camp, and of the 200 Turks no more than 40 survived. The victors then poured into the camp and slaughtered everyone they met except women and children.

At the Battle of Wofla on 28 August 1542, Imam Ahmad crushed a Portuguese expeditionary force, killing most of its men and capturing practically all of the firearms they had. He also captured and killed its leader, Cristóvão da Gama, whom he beheaded. Armies in the Horn of Africa melted away with the death of their leaders.

From 1557 the Ottoman Empire occupied parts of Ethiopia and set up Habesh Eyalet, the province of Abyssinia. It was created by conquering Massawa, Ethiopia's main port, and by seizing Suakin from the Ethiopian-allied Funj Sultanate in what is now Sudan.

In 1573 the Adal Sultanate tried to invade Ethiopia again, but Sarsa Dengel defended the frontier at the Battle of Webi River. He defeated, captured and executed the Adalite Sultan Muhammad ibn Nasir along with the core of the Adalite nobility. This marked the end of Adal as a military power.

After the Ethiopian empire's decline, the deaths of Emperor Iyasu II in 1755 and Iyoas I in 1769 led to the Zemene Mesafint, a period of decentralization. Regional warlords fought for power, and the emperor was a mere puppet.

Emperor Iyasu the Great, who reigned from 1682 to 1706, resumed the offensive against the Oromo and recruited Oromo battalions that pledged allegiance to him. Tulama and Liban Oromo were settled in northern Gojjam and Begemder and were encouraged to convert to Christianity.

At Shimbra Kure in March 1529, Imam Ahmad's Adal troops defeated a larger Ethiopian contingent. The Harari cavalry, also known as the Malassay, proved instrumental as the Abyssinian troops were outmaneuvered. Ethiopian chronicles mark this year as the start of what they call the persecution. Later the Adalites sacked and burned numerous churches, including Atronsa Maryam, where the remains of several Emperors had been interred, and at Aksum the Imam killed a large number of the Tigrayans who had assembled to defend the city; an Arab chronicler estimates over 10,000 Christians were killed.

In April 1542 the Portuguese met Imam Ahmad's army at Antalo, his first engagement against an enemy equipped with cannon. Ahmad was wounded and his horse killed under him. He appealed to Zabid for help, promising to become a vassal of Sultan Suleiman I, and Ottoman forces answered with ten field guns and 700 soldiers.

Before the 1543 battle, Emperor Galawdewos advised waiting for 50 missing Portuguese soldiers, since in that country fifty Portuguese were said to be a greater reinforcement than one thousand natives. Cavalry raids followed, until the Imam's camp killed the leading Ethiopian soldier, Azmach Keflo, which demoralized the Ethiopian troops. Faced with possible desertion, Galawdewos attacked the next day. Earlier, on 13 February 1543, the allied army had killed the Imam's lieutenant Sayid Mehmed at Wogera.

In 1709, Wallo Oromo invaded the Amba of Atronsa Maryam in Saynt, a prominent royal monastery, scattering its historic relics, killing its clergy and carrying away women and children as prisoners. They even tossed the disputed picture of the Virgin and Child and the bones of the fifteenth-century emperor Ba'eda Maryam, who was buried in the Amba, over the steep cliff.

After the Portuguese recaptured Fort Jesus in 1632, they refurbished it and built more fortifications, which made it harder for the fort to fall. Even so, Omani Arabs led by Saif bin Sultan besieged it from 1696 to 1698 and took it, ending the Portuguese presence on the coast.

After Wofla, Imam Ahmad reduced his mercenary Ottoman arquebusiers to 200. A Hadhrami chronicle says some threatened his life unless he gave them 10,000 ounces of gold, which he granted. When the rest of the group made a similar demand, he decided he no longer needed their services and sent them home with 2,000 ounces instead.

The Portuguese besieged and took Amba Sanayti in central Tigray in February 1542, after wintering with Empress Sabla Wangel at Debre Damo. On 28 August 1542, Cristóvão da Gama was wounded, captured and killed along with thirteen of his men on Ahmad's own order, possibly at Wofla itself. About half the Portuguese company died in the fighting, and the Portuguese had already been reduced by the loss of fifty to a hundred men. The survivors made their way to Semien and joined Gelawdewos in October 1542.

literature.text: Around 1593, the Ethiopian monk Abba Bahrey wrote The History of the Galla in Ge'ez. It told of the Oromo people and their 16th-century migration into what is now central and western Ethiopia. It is the only documentation of the Oromo in that century.

In the 17th century, the Ethiopian thinker Zera Yacob wrote a philosophical treatise called the Hatata, meaning 'inquiry'. Scholars have compared his inquiry to the work of Descartes. Zera Yacob was critical of all religions, including his own Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Ethiopian literary works were mostly handwritten codices called branna, made by gathering parchment leaves and sewing them together. Another kind of written object was the protective scroll, which served as a written amulet. Debtera, non-ordained clergy who were experts on exorcism and healing, typically produced these scrolls.

Royal chronicles were a major Ethiopian literary genre, recounting kings' administration and military campaigns. They were used to legitimize the Solomonic dynasty, much as the Kebra Nagast did. That book is probably the best-known piece of Ethiopian literature.
Bahrey was both a historian and an ethnographer. Besides his work on the Oromo, he wrote The History of King Sarsa Dengel, which chronicles the reign of that emperor.
tags: The History of King Sarsa Dengel

literature.text: Abba 'Enbaqom wrote a letter to Imam Ahmad Ibn Ibrahim titled Anqasa Amin, or 'Gate of the Faith', giving his reasons for abandoning Islam. It was probably first written in Arabic and rewritten in an expanded Ge'ez version around 1532. It is considered one of the classics of later Ge'ez literature.

According to the first Hatata, Zara Yaqob fled his hometown of Aksum around 1630 because of religious persecution. It came from the Portuguese Jesuits and from Emperor Susenyos I, who had converted to Catholicism in 1622. He writes that he lived in a cave for two years, and penned the text more than thirty years later, in 1668.

Zera Yacob had a disciple, Walda Heywat, who also wrote a philosophical treatise systematising his master's thought. Walda Heywat paid more attention to practical and educational problems. His work is arguably less original but can be considered 'more Ethiopian', since it joins Zera Yacob's ideas with traditional Christian-inspired wisdom.

Ethiopian sapiential literature preferred narrative, parable, apothegm and rich imagery to abstract argument. It included translations and adaptations of Greek texts, among them The Book of the Wise Philosophers (1510/22).
tags: The Book of the Wise Philosophers

literature.text: After crushing the Beta Israel revolt, Emperor Susenyos I confiscated their lands and forcibly baptized them. He forbade the practice of Judaism and ordered his men to 'erase the memory of the Jews', which meant mass killing, looting and the burning of their belongings and holy books. As a result, much traditional Jewish culture and practice was lost or changed, including the Hebrew language.

Ethiopian tradition credits Yared with composing the liturgical hymns and the notation system called meleket. A 16th-century royal chronicle instead credits two clerics with the system. This, along with differences between Christian and Jewish traditions, suggests Yared was not responsible.

In 2017, Getatchew Haile, a leading scholar of Ge'ez studies, changed his long-held view of the Hatatas. He had long rejected their authenticity. He wrote that he now believed the original Hatata was the work of an Ethiopian debtera who lived during the reign of Emperor Susenyos, 1607-32.

science.text: Emperor Fasilides is credited with building seven stone bridges across Ethiopia, including the Sebara Dildiy bridge. Because of this legacy, old bridges throughout the country are still often popularly attributed to him.

In the early seventeenth century, the Portuguese missionary Manoel de Almeida reported that Lake Tana held 21 islands, several of which he said were 'formerly large, but now much diminished.' Seven or eight of these islands had monasteries on them.

Fort Jesus in Mombasa was the first European-style fort built outside Europe to be designed to resist cannon fire. It was designed by the Milanese architect Giovanni Battista Cairati, who was Chief Architect for Portuguese possessions in the East.

The Jesuit Pedro Páez is credited as the first European to see and describe the source of the Blue Nile, which he reached on 21 April 1618. His two-volume História da Etiópia is regarded as one of the most valuable and accurate works on the Ethiopian empire of his time.

In the late eighteenth century, James Bruce visited Lake Tana and was told by locals that it held 45 inhabited islands. He doubted this account, judging that the true number was probably closer to eleven.

Fort Jesus is roughly square, with four bulwarks at its corners, and was built in the shape of a man viewed from the air. Although its design is an example of Renaissance architecture, it is considered a masterpiece of late Renaissance military fortification.

Cairati drew his inspiration from the Italian architect Pietro Cataneo, and Gaspar Rodrigues was the master builder. Although the design was European, the masonry techniques, building materials and labor are believed to have been provided by the local Swahili people.

The number of islands in Lake Tana varies with the water level of the lake. Over the last 400 years that level has fallen about 2 metres, which helps explain why early visitors counted such different numbers of islands.

politics.text: Adal, a tributary of Ethiopia, invaded the Ethiopian Empire in 1531 with the support of the Ottoman Empire and other Muslim peoples in the region. The war lasted until 1543, and Ethiopia was able to reclaim its lost territory and win only with the help of the Portuguese Empire and Cristóvão da Gama. Both the Christian and Muslim regions of Ethiopia were significantly weakened by the war, which has been suggested as a possible factor in the Oromo migrations of the 16th century.

From 1769 to 1855, Ethiopia passed through the Princes Era, or Zemene Mesafint. Various Ras fought constantly with the Emperor, who had only limited power and dominated just the area around Gondar. Religious conflict was often used as a pretext for strife.

Under Iyasu the Great (1682-1706), Ethiopia dispatched embassies to Louis XIV's France and to Dutch India. His reign was a major period of consolidation within an era of intense cultural and artistic creation.

The first continuous relations between Ethiopia and a European country began in 1508 with Portugal, under Emperor Lebna Dengel. When Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi attacked, Portugal sent weapons and four hundred men. They helped Lebna Dengel's son Gelawdewos defeat Ahmad and re-establish his rule.

In 1557, Özdemir Pasha took the port of Massawa for the Ottoman Empire, beginning a war that lasted until 1589. His force of 3,000 janissaries and 1,000 horsemen funded its fort at Debarwa through looting, extractions on trade and a poll tax on the local population. The Ottomans never gained effective long-term control beyond the port and island where they were directly present, and Massawa and the nearby coast were soon transferred to Beja Na'ibs, or deputies.

Oromo groups expanded across the region in the 16th and 17th centuries. Between 1620 and 1660, Ethiopian emperors had to defend different parts of their territory but could not stop the waves of advancing Oromo groups. In 1642 the eastern Oromo nearly annihilated the Ethiopian army from Tigray. Under emperors Fasiladas and Yohannes II, the Oromo seem to have been virtually unrestrained in their expansion.

From 1769 to 1855, Ethiopia passed through the Princes Era, or Zemene Mesafint, when various Ras fought the Emperor, who had limited power. The development of society and culture stagnated, and religious conflict, including within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, was often used as a pretext for strife.

In 1576, Emperor Sarsa Dengel liquidated a massive invading Adalite army at the Battle of Webi River. He captured and executed the Adalite Sultan along with the core of the Adalite nobility. This permanently extinguished Adal as a military power.

During Emperor Tewoflos's reign (1708-1711), a revolt in Gojjam led by Tege, who organized a large number of Oromos of the Liban, Baso and Qalaganda factions, was put down at Yebaba. Tewoflos then ordered the burning of more than five hundred Oromos who had entered the church of Dabra Mawi'e nearby. According to the chronicle, none of them escaped alive to tell the story.

In 1577, Muhammad Gasa moved the capital of Adal from Harar to Aussa because of pressure from the Oromo invasions. This founded the Imamate of Aussa. In 1769, the Mudaito dynasty of Afar in Aussa overthrew the Kabirto of Harla and Doba, who were descended from the Walasma dynasty.

philosophy.text: In the 17th century, Zera Yacob (1599–1692) became the most important figure of an Ethiopian philosophical renaissance. His treatise Hatata, written in 1667, is often included in the narrow canon of universal philosophy.

Zera Yacob, an Ethiopian philosopher born in 1600, wrote a treatise called Hatata, meaning "The Inquiry". It explores reason, morality and religious tolerance. He argued for following one's natural reasoning instead of believing what one is told by others.

Scholars have compared Zera Yacob's inquiry to that of Descartes. One major difference is that Zera Yacob was critical towards all religions, including his own Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The Catholic Descartes, by contrast, followed a more traditional religious perspective.

Around 1510, Abba Mikael translated and adapted the Arabic Book of the Wise Philosophers into Geʽez. It was a collection of sayings from the early Greek pre-Socratics, Plato and Aristotle, passed down through neo-Platonic dialogues. It was also influenced by Arab philosophy and Ethiopian discussions.

Zera Yacob was born into a farming family near Aksum in Tigray. His father was poor but supported his attendance at traditional schools, where he learned the Psalms of David and the Ethiopian Orthodox Christian faith. He was denounced before Emperor Susenyos I, who had turned to Roman Catholicism and ordered his subjects to follow his example. Zera Yacob refused to adopt the Catholic faith and fled into exile with some gold and the Book of Psalms.

According to the first Hatata, Zara Yaqob fled Aksum around 1630 to escape religious persecution by the Portuguese Jesuits and Emperor Susenyos I. He writes that he lived in a cave for two years. He penned the text more than thirty years later, in 1668.

Susenyos I made Roman Catholicism the official state religion but met heavy resistance from his subjects and the Ethiopian Orthodox authorities. He abdicated in 1632 in favour of his son Fasilides. Fasilides promptly restored Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity and expelled the Jesuits in 1633.

Zera Yacob became the teacher of Habtu's two sons. At the request of his patron's son Walda Heywat, he wrote his famous 1668 treatise on the light of reason. He is believed to have remained in Emfraz for the next 25 years and died there in 1693.

Although Zera Yacob was of humble birth, he earned respect for his intellectual capacities and pursued the traditional Ethiopian theological education. He mastered Coptic and Catholic theology, knew Jewish and Islamic religions well, and sought comfort and inspiration in David's Book of Psalms.

After Fasilides took power, Zera Yacob left his cave and settled in Emfraz, where a rich merchant named Habta Egziabher, known as Habtu, became his patron. He refused to live as a monk, saying the law of Christians ranking monastic life above marriage was false. He also rejected polygamy, because the law of creation orders one man to marry one woman.

Walda Heywat was Zera Yacob's disciple and wrote his own treatise, systematising his master's thought. He paid more attention to practical and educational problems. He often drew on parables, many of them from the Book of the Wise Philosophers, making his work "more Ethiopian" though arguably less original.

Zera Yacob's ideas were relatively individualistic, but his disciple Walda Heywat was a social ethicist. He wrote that God did not create him only for himself, but placed him among other created men who are equal to him. He also said a man cannot come to existence, grow and serve by himself without the help of others.

In late 2023, De Gruyter published the first English translation of the Hatata texts outside of Ethiopia. Getatchew Haile, a leading Geʽez scholar who long rejected the Hatatas' authenticity, had already written in 2017 that he was inclined to believe the original Hatata was the work of an Ethiopian debtera from the era of Susenyos.

culture.text: When Emperor Susenyos converted to Roman Catholicism in 1624, years of revolt and civil unrest followed, with thousands of deaths. On 25 June 1632, his son Fasilides declared the state religion to be Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity again and expelled the Jesuit missionaries and other Europeans.

In 1669–1670, Emperor Yohannes I ordered Muslims and Jews to separate from Christians and form their own sectors in Gondar. By 1676 Muslims had settled in the lower town in a quarter called Eslam Bet, and the Beta Israel were given four quarters, including Abarra and Kayla Meda.

Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity has long been central to Amhara culture. Easter and Epiphany are the most important celebrations, marked with services, feasting and dancing, and many fast days through the year allow only vegetables or fish to be eaten.

The French physician Charles Poncet served Emperor Iyasu I at Gondar and wrote extensively about the city at the end of the seventeenth century. He was the first European observer to describe Gondar, whose existence some in Europe had doubted.

In the 17th century, King Suseynos adopted Catholicism, and Jesuit missionaries arrived in Ethiopia. His attempt to force Catholicism on his people challenged Ethiopian religious beliefs and inspired further development of Ethiopian philosophy.

Much of the labour on the royal buildings at Gondar was supplied by the Beta Israel, particularly the Kayla clan. They traditionally worked as masons, metalsmiths and carpenters, trades that the general population regarded as low in repute.

Fasilides built some of the earliest of Gondar's fabled 44 churches, including Adababay Iyasus, Atatami Mikael and Gemjabet Mariyam. In 1665 he ordered the "Books of the Franks", the remaining religious writings of the Catholics, to be burnt.

At Epiphany, called Timkat, the Tabot, a model of the Ark of the Covenant, is wrapped in rich cloth and carried in procession on a priest's head. Water is blessed near dawn and sprinkled on participants, some of whom immerse themselves to renew their baptismal vows.

Under Emperor Iyasu I, Oromo groups who pledged allegiance were settled in conquered areas. The Tulama and Liban Oromo were settled in northern Gojjam and Begemder and encouraged to convert to Christianity, and some of their leaders were given high army and provincial offices.

When Armenian Khoja Murad visited the imperial palace at Gondar in 1696, he claimed there were at least 80 royal children who "ran around indiscriminately". The palace served as the residence of the royal family.
